slides.title: Food tests: lab tips
slides.oldHtml:
Food tests: lab tips for clear results

PREP FIRST: Crush solid foods with ~5–10 cm³ water (let bits settle or filter) — use only ~2 cm³ per tube — avoid dark foods (e.g. beetroot, soy sauce) that hide colours — keep glassware clean
Starch — Iodine
  • Use a white spotting tile so blue-black stands out
  • Only 2–3 drops of iodine on a tiny piece or drop — instant
  • Best foods: potato, bread, rice, pasta (not sugar!)
Glucose — Benedict’s
  • Equal volumes: ~2 cm³ food + ~2 cm³ Benedict’s
  • Heat in a ~80 °C water bath for 5 min (no direct Bunsen)
  • Best foods: apple juice, honey, onion (not table sucrose!)
Protein — Biuret
  • Add ~2 cm³ biuret to ~2 cm³ sample, shake gently (no heat)
  • Hold against white paper — weak positives are pale lilac
  • Best foods: egg white, milk, tofu, grated cheese
Lipids — Emulsion
  • Ethanol first (~2 cm³) + tiny smear, shake hard to dissolve fat
  • Then pour into ~2 cm³ cold water (keep ethanol off flames!)
  • Best foods: cooking oil, butter, crushed nut or sunflower seed

Food tests: lab tips

PREP FIRST: Crush solid foods with ~5–10 mL water (let bits settle or filter) — use only ~2 mL per tube — avoid dark foods (e.g. beetroot, soy sauce) that hide colours — keep glassware clean
Starch — Iodine
  • Use a white spotting tile so blue-black stands out
  • Only 2–3 drops of iodine on a tiny piece or drop — instant
  • Best foods: potato, bread, rice, pasta (not sugar!)
Glucose — Benedict’s
  • Equal volumes: ~2 mL food + ~2 mL Benedict’s
  • Heat in a ~80 °C water bath for 5 min (no direct Bunsen)
  • Best foods: apple juice, honey, onion (not table sucrose!)
Protein — Biuret
  • Add ~2 mL biuret to ~2 mL sample, shake gently (no heat)
  • Hold against white paper — weak positives are pale lilac
  • Best foods: egg white, milk, tofu, grated cheese
Lipids — Emulsion
  • Ethanol first (~2 mL) + tiny smear, shake hard to dissolve fat
  • Then pour into ~2 mL cold water (keep ethanol off flames!)
  • Best foods: cooking oil, butter, crushed nut or sunflower seed
🧪 Teacher prep: making Biuret from CuSO₄(aq) + NaOH(aq)
Best bench method: 2 separate bottles (no precipitate!)
  • Biuret A (alkali): 5–10% NaOH(aq) (~1–2 M; or 0.4 M / 16 g/L for lower-hazard KS4)
  • Biuret B (dilute copper sulfate): 0.5–1% CuSO₄(aq) (5–10 g CuSO₄·5H₂O per L — pale sky-blue; or dilute 1 M stock 1 : 25 with water)
  • Class steps: Add ~2 mL NaOH(aq) to ~2 mL sample, swirl, then add 3–5 drops CuSO₄(aq) & shake gently → lilac/purple
⚠ Don’t mix plain CuSO₄ + NaOH in one bottle!
Plain Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ immediately precipitates insoluble blue Cu(OH)₂(s). To pre-mix 1 L in one bottle you need a chelator: dissolve 1.5 g CuSO₄·5H₂O + 6 g Rochelle salt (Na K tartrate) in 500 mL water, stir in 300 mL 10% NaOH, top up to 1 L.
Safety & pro tips
Goggles mandatory (NaOH is corrosive) · keep CuSO₄ very pale blue (too dark masks faint lilac) · best control = 1 part egg white : 4 parts water (swirl gently, don’t froth).

slides.title: Types of attraction
slides.oldHtml:
Types of attraction

Intermolecular: weak attractions between molecules
Ionic: strong attraction between + and − ions
Covalent: strong shared pair of electrons
slides.newHtml:
Types of attraction

Intermolecular forces
Weak attractions between separate molecules
Ionic bonding
Strong attraction between + and − ions
Covalent bonding
Strong shared pair of electrons

slides.title: Metals and non-metals
slides.oldHtml:
Metals and non-metals

Where are the non-metals?
  • Top right of the Periodic Table (blue) — plus Hydrogen (H)
  • Covalent bonds only form between non-metals
  • Metals (red) + non-metals → ionic
slides.newHtml:
Metals and non-metals

Non-metal + Non-metal → Covalent (share e⁻)
Metal + Non-metal → Ionic (transfer e⁻)

slides.title: Intermolecular forces in water
slides.oldHtml:
Intermolecular forces in water

Inside each H₂O
Strong covalent bonds hold H and O together — these do not break when water boils
Dotted lines between H₂O
Weak intermolecular forces pull molecules together — boiling only overcomes these

Between H₂O molecules

slides.title: Giant covalent structures
slides.oldHtml:
Giant covalent structures

Millions of non-metal atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
  • Like a giant ionic lattice, but with no charged ions
  • Very high melting & boiling points (lots of energy to break bonds)
  • Insoluble in water — no conduction (except graphite)
Why is Carbon so good at this?
Carbon (Group 4) has 4 outer electrons → forms up to 4 strong covalent bonds in every direction to build giant networks! (Silicon does too, e.g. quartz SiO₂.)
Each carbon shares electrons with 4 neighbours
Quartz (SiO₂) — giant covalent too
